title: Scene entity ids are resolved by each adapter, never by mapSceneEntity
observation: Catalyst deployment events from the event-driven SNS bus were silently discarded: mapSceneEntity read entity.id, but the bus sends the CatalystDeployment shape from @dcl/schemas/misc (entityId, entityType, authChain, optional metadata) rather than the full Entity, and handleCatalystDeployment passed no fallback id.
conclusion: mapSceneEntity takes a REQUIRED sceneId argument and reads no id key of its own. Each adapter resolves the id from its own payload with pickString and passes the value: deployment-consumer from entity.entityId / entity.id / event.key, worlds-content-server from item.entityId or item.entity.id, catalyst-content from activeEntity.id. Never add a producer-specific key branch to the shared parser.
rejected: teaching mapSceneEntity to read id ?? entityId itself
rationale: Content-addressed /contents/{entityId} bodies carry no id under any key (the id is the file hash), so an accessor has nothing to reach for on the worlds path and a separate fallbackId parameter would survive alongside it. Reading both keys inside the parser makes it accumulate one branch per producer. A required parameter turns the omitted-id mistake that caused this bug into a compile error instead of a production log line.

title: Never list-and-filter a paginated upstream for a permission decision
observation: getScenes(worldName) called GET /world/:name/scenes with no pagination. Upstream builds that route with getPaginationParams, whose limit defaults AND caps at 100, so only the first page was ever read: a collaborator on scene #101 of a world was denied storage access. It fails closed, so no error, no alert, and no test caught it because no test world has 100 scenes.
conclusion: Authorization here is always single-parcel (the parcel comes from the signed fetch metadata), so ask the upstream for the scene at that parcel rather than for the list. Worlds: POST /world/:name/scenes with {coordinates:[parcel]}. Genesis: POST /entities/active with {pointers:[parcel]}. Neither route requires a signature, and neither response paginates for a single parcel. Check the upstream default limit before calling any list endpoint in an authorization path.
rejected: paginating getScenes with a limit/offset loop until total is reached
rationale: Pagination would make the wrong query correct. The caller wants the scene at one parcel, so walking every page of a world to filter it down is slower, still coupled to the page size, and answers a much larger question than the authorization decision needs. Upstream itself uses the coordinates filter to authorize its own undeploys.

title: No orphan files under src/logic or src/adapters - everything there is a component
observation: src/logic/logs-permissions.ts was flagged in review as an orphan file. It was first folded into src/logic/scene-entity.ts, which is itself an orphan file, so the rule was still broken - the fix moved orphan content between orphans. The reviewer's actual rule is that every module under the component directories must be a component.
conclusion: src/logic/** and src/adapters/** contain only component directories: component.ts + types.ts + index.ts, built by an async create*Component factory, registered in src/components.ts, declared on BaseComponents in src/types/system.ts, and consumed through Pick<AppComponents, ...>. Dependency-free helpers belong in src/utils/, which sits outside the component directories. Split by nature: parsing primitives (isRecord, pickString) are utils; domain rules (mapSceneEntity, normalizeTitle, extractLogsPermissions) are a component. A helper that runs before any component exists, like the pg connection string builder, is also a util.
rejected: folding an orphan helper into another orphan file
keeping dependency-free helpers as loose files under src/logic
rationale: A loose file under a component directory has no interface, no registration and no seam to substitute in tests. Moving orphan content between orphan files looks like a fix but leaves the same violation in place, which is exactly what happened on the first attempt.
